name: Ancient Capitals & Khmer Civilization
nameKh: តំបន់អតីតរាជធានី និងអរិយធម៌ខ្មែរ
tagline: The center of Khmer civilization — from Mahendraparvata to Chaktomuk.
summary: Angkor, Sambor Prei Kuk and the royal capitals that came before them — temple complexes, inscriptions and the long arc of Khmer statecraft.
aboutTitle: Discover the Rise of Khmer Civilization
aboutTitleKh: ស្វែងយល់ពីការរុងរឿងនៃអរិយធម៌ខ្មែរ
coreIdentity: The historical heart of Khmer civilization — the line you can walk from one royal capital to the next, and with it the evolution of religion, architecture, public infrastructure, and cultural heritage from Chenla to the modern kingdom.
coreIdentityKh: ជាបេះដូងប្រវត្តិសាស្ត្រនៃអរិយធម៌ខ្មែរ — ជាខ្សែដែលអ្នកអាចដើរតាមពីរាជធានីមួយទៅរាជធានីមួយទៀត និងតាមនោះឃើញការវិវឌ្ឍនៃសាសនា ស្ថាបត្យកម្ម ហេដ្ឋារចនាសម្ព័ន្ធសាធារណៈ និងបេតិកភណ្ឌវប្បធម៌ ចាប់ពីសម័យចេនឡារហូតដល់រាជាណាចក្របច្ចុប្បន្ន។
highlightIntro: The succession of royal capitals this region is built around — read it top to bottom.

highlights.label: c. 600 – 700 CE
highlights.title: Ishanapura
highlights.subtitle: Sambor Prei Kuk
highlights.description: Capital of Chenla under Isanavarman I, and the first place Khmer temple architecture settled into a form of its own.

highlights.label: 802 – c. 835 CE
highlights.title: Mahendraparvata
highlights.subtitle: Phnom Kulen
highlights.titleKh: មហេន្ទ្របវ៌ត
highlights.description: The mountain city where Jayavarman II declared himself universal monarch in 802, the act that begins the Angkorian era.

highlights.label: c. 835 – 889 CE
highlights.title: Hariharalaya
highlights.subtitle: Roluos
highlights.description: The plain below the mountain, where Indravarman I built the first state temple and the first great reservoir.

highlights.label: 889 – c. 1431 CE
highlights.title: Yasodharapura
highlights.subtitle: Angkor
highlights.description: Five centuries of capital on one site — Angkor Wat, Angkor Thom, and the largest pre-industrial city in the world.

highlights.label: 928 – 944 CE
highlights.title: Lingapura
highlights.subtitle: Koh Ker
highlights.description: Jayavarman IV moved the court a hundred kilometres north-east and raised a seven-tier pyramid. It lasted sixteen years.

highlights.label: 1528 – 1594 CE
highlights.title: Longvek
highlights.description: The walled river capital of Ang Chan I, at the centre of Cambodia's maritime trade with China and the Malay world.

highlights.label: 1618 – 1866 CE
highlights.title: Oudong
highlights.description: Two and a half centuries of capital on a low ridge, crowned by the stupas of the kings buried there.

highlights.label: 1866 CE – present
highlights.title: Chaktomuk
highlights.subtitle: Phnom Penh
highlights.description: The capital returns to the four-rivers junction it first held in 1434. Norodom I builds the Royal Palace here in 1866.

name: Northeastern Civilization
nameKh: តំបន់អរិយធម៌ឦសាន
tagline: Crater lakes, forest and indigenous country east of the Mekong.
summary: Highland provinces where indigenous communities, crater lakes and forest trails sit well off the temple trail.
aboutTitle: Meet the Highlands on Their Own Terms
coreIdentity: The upland provinces where Bunong, Tampuan, Jarai, Kreung and Brao communities keep their own languages, calendars and forests — the part of Cambodia the temple trail never reaches, reached instead by red roads, longtail boats and the two rivers that drain it.
highlightIntro: The highlands are not one culture but several. These are the communities whose land, language and forest this region is built around.

highlights.label: Mondulkiri
highlights.title: Bunong
highlights.description: The largest highland community in the country, and the reason Mondulkiri's forest, elephants and rotational farmland are still held collectively.

highlights.label: Ratanakiri
highlights.title: Tampuan
highlights.description: The villages around Banlung, and the community that owns and protects the Yeak Laom crater lake.

highlights.label: Ratanakiri
highlights.title: Jarai
highlights.description: Austronesian speakers along the Sesan and the Vietnamese border, related in language to the Cham of the lowlands.

highlights.label: Ratanakiri
highlights.title: Kreung
highlights.description: Known for the layout of their villages around a communal house, and for burial grounds carved with figures of the dead.

highlights.label: Ratanakiri
highlights.title: Brao
highlights.description: River people of the upper Sesan around Ta Veng, whose territory runs across into southern Laos.

highlights.label: Ratanakiri
highlights.title: Kavet
highlights.description: The far north-east, in and around what is now Virachey National Park — among the most remote settlements in Cambodia.

highlights.label: Ratanakiri
highlights.title: Kachok
highlights.description: A small community east of Banlung, farming the basalt uplands between the Sesan and the Srepok.

highlights.label: Mondulkiri · Kratié
highlights.title: Stieng
highlights.description: The south-western edge of the highlands, where the plateau drops towards the Mekong plain.

name: Mekong & Tonle Sap Civilization
nameKh: តំបន់អរិយធម៌មេគង្គ និងទន្លេសាប
tagline: The lake that reverses, and the river that feeds it.
summary: Life shaped by water — floating villages, flooded forest, river dolphins and the lake that reverses its flow each year.
coreIdentity: A whole culture built on a flood pulse. Once a year the Tonle Sap river turns and runs backwards, the lake swells to five times its size, and everything that lives on it — villages, forests, fishing grounds, the calendar itself — moves with the water and then moves back.
highlightIntro: This region is organised by a single annual cycle rather than by history. Read it top to bottom and you have the year.

highlights.label: December – April
highlights.title: The lake at its smallest
highlights.titleKh: រដូវប្រាំង
highlights.description: Around 2,500 km² and barely a metre deep. Boats need channels dug for them, and the villages follow the shoreline out across the mud.

highlights.label: May – June
highlights.title: The monsoon arrives
highlights.description: The upstream Mekong begins to rise, fed by snowmelt off the Tibetan plateau and the first of the south-west monsoon.

highlights.label: Late May – June
highlights.title: The river turns back
highlights.titleKh: ទន្លេសាបបញ្ច្រាស
highlights.description: The Mekong pushes harder than the lake can drain, and the Tonle Sap river reverses to run north — one of the few rivers on earth that changes direction each year.

highlights.label: July – September
highlights.title: The flooded forest goes under
highlights.description: Water spreads into the ring of freshwater swamp forest around the lake, which becomes the nursery for most of the fish in the system.

highlights.label: September – October
highlights.title: The lake at its largest
highlights.description: Up to five times its dry-season area and as much as nine metres deep, spilling across five provinces.

highlights.label: October – November
highlights.title: The river turns south again
highlights.titleKh: បុណ្យអុំទូក
highlights.description: The flow reverses back towards the Mekong, and the country marks it with Bon Om Touk — three days of longboat racing on the full moon.

highlights.label: October – March
highlights.title: The fish come out with the water
highlights.description: The dai fishery strings stationary nets across the Tonle Sap river to meet the migration draining out of the lake.

highlights.label: Since 1997
highlights.title: Protected, on paper
highlights.description: UNESCO listed the lake as a Biosphere Reserve with three core areas — Prek Toal, Boeung Tonle Chhmar and Stung Sen.

name: Mountain & Waterfall Region
nameKh: តំបន់ភ្នំ និងទឹកធ្លាក់
tagline: Cardamom ridgelines, plateau pine and the falls after the rains.
summary: Cardamom ridgelines, cool plateau air and the cascades that run hardest at the tail end of the rains.
coreIdentity: The high ground of the south-west and the water that comes off it — rainforest massifs holding the largest intact forest in mainland South-East Asia, a French hill station in the cloud, limestone caves with shrines inside them, and cascades that only truly run for half the year.
highlightIntro: Cambodia is mostly floodplain. This region is the exception — the uplands that ring it, and the water that comes off them.

highlights.label: Koh Kong · Pursat
highlights.title: Cardamom Mountains
highlights.titleKh: ជួរភ្នំក្រវាញ
highlights.description: The largest intact rainforest in mainland South-East Asia, still holding elephant, gaur and clouded leopard, and still being surveyed.

highlights.label: Kampong Speu
highlights.title: Phnom Aural
highlights.titleKh: ភ្នំឧរ៉ាល់
highlights.description: The summit of the country, on the eastern edge of the Cardamom massif — a hard two-day climb through leech forest.

highlights.label: Kampot · Koh Kong
highlights.title: Elephant Mountains
highlights.titleKh: ជួរភ្នំដំរី
highlights.description: The Damrei range running down to the Gulf, topped by the Bokor plateau and the hill station the French abandoned twice.

highlights.label: Kampong Speu
highlights.title: Kirirom
highlights.description: A pine-covered shelf high enough to be cold at night, and the closest highland to Phnom Penh.

highlights.label: Preah Vihear · Oddar Meanchey
highlights.title: Dangrek Mountains
highlights.titleKh: ជួរភ្នំដងរែក
highlights.description: The cliff line marking the Thai border, with Preah Vihear temple laid along the top of it at 525 m.

highlights.label: Siem Reap
highlights.title: Phnom Kulen
highlights.description: The quarry that built Angkor and the mountain where the empire was declared, with the falls and riverbed carvings on top.

highlights.label: Battambang · Kampot
highlights.title: The Limestone Outcrops
highlights.description: Isolated karst hills standing out of the paddy, hollow with caves that have held shrines for more than a thousand years.

name: Coastal & Island Region
nameKh: តំបន់ឆ្នេរ និងកោះ
tagline: Fishing ports, mangrove estuaries and a boat ride offshore.
summary: The Gulf of Thailand coastline: fishing ports, mangrove estuaries and islands a short boat ride offshore.
coreIdentity: Around 443 km of Gulf coastline and some sixty islands off it — from resort bays with a ferry every hour to islands running on one generator, held together by the mangrove systems that feed the whole fishery.
highlightIntro: Four provinces and four island groups, in the order you would travel them from the Thai border down to the Vietnamese one.

highlights.label: Koh Kong
highlights.title: The Border Corner
highlights.description: Estuaries and standing mangrove where the Cardamoms come down to the sea, plus the country's largest island offshore.

highlights.label: Koh Kong
highlights.title: Koh Sdach Archipelago
highlights.description: A working cluster of small islands off Botum Sakor, still more fishing village than resort.

highlights.label: Preah Sihanouk
highlights.title: Sihanoukville
highlights.description: The deep-water port, the mainland beaches either side of it, and every ferry to the islands.

highlights.label: Preah Sihanouk
highlights.title: Koh Rong Archipelago
highlights.description: The main island group — Koh Rong, Koh Rong Sanloem, Koh Ta Kiev and Koh Russei, half an hour to two hours out.

highlights.label: Preah Sihanouk
highlights.title: The Outer Islands
highlights.description: Koh Tang and Koh Prins, four hours offshore, with the clearest water and the only wreck diving in Cambodian waters.

highlights.label: Kampot
highlights.title: The Kampot Estuary
highlights.description: No real beach here — a river mouth, salt pans worked by hand, and the Bokor range standing behind it all.

highlights.label: Kep
highlights.title: Kep
highlights.description: A single bay, a crab market on stilts, and the ruins of the villas the coast was built around in the 1960s.

highlights.label: Kep
highlights.title: Kep Archipelago
highlights.description: Thirteen islands with the country's best surviving seagrass beds, and the marine reserve rebuilding them.

name: Urban Lifestyle & Nightlife
nameKh: តំបន់រស់នៅទីក្រុង និងជីវិតរាត្រី
tagline: Rooftops, night markets and kitchens that stay open late.
summary: City rhythms after dark — rooftop bars, riverside markets, live music and kitchens that stay open late.
coreIdentity: What the towns do once the heat drops — riverside promenades that fill at six, night markets, live music in converted shophouses, art schools founded by returning refugees, and a bar scene that runs from plastic stools on the pavement to the top of the newest tower.
highlightIntro: Six towns, each with its own evening. What follows is what the night actually looks like in each of them.

highlights.label: Phnom Penh
highlights.title: Four rivers, all hours
highlights.description: The riverside fills an hour before dark, the rooftops open above it, and the food lanes off Street 308 keep going long after both.

highlights.label: Siem Reap
highlights.title: Pub Street and everything behind it
highlights.description: The loudest strip in the country, with the boutique lanes of Kandal Village and the circus tent a few blocks away.

highlights.label: Battambang
highlights.title: Circus and shophouses
highlights.description: The best-preserved colonial streets in Cambodia, and the arts school that trained most of the country's performers.

highlights.label: Kampot
highlights.title: Slow evenings on the water
highlights.description: Sunset boats, a music school reviving pre-war Khmer repertoire, and bars that close when the last person leaves.

highlights.label: Preah Sihanouk
highlights.title: The coast after dark
highlights.titleKh: ក្រុងព្រះសីហនុ
highlights.description: A working deep-water port, a night market beside it, and the beach bars strung out along Otres.

highlights.label: Kep
highlights.title: Dinner and nothing else
highlights.description: The quietest of the six on purpose — the crab market at dusk is the whole evening, and that is the appeal.

name: Khmer Culinary Region
nameKh: តំបន់មុខម្ហូបខ្មែរ
tagline: Prahok and pepper, market breakfasts and producer visits.
summary: Where the eating is the itinerary: prahok and Kampot pepper, market breakfasts, home kitchens and producer visits.
aboutTitle: Eat Your Way Across the Country
coreIdentity: Cambodian food where it is actually made — the pepper terraces and palm-sugar kilns that hold the country's only protected-origin products, the fermenting jars of prahok that underpin nearly every savoury dish, and the provincial cooking that never travelled to the capital.
highlightIntro: Six ingredients and dishes explain most of what you will be served. Learn these and the rest of the menu makes sense.

highlights.label: Nationwide
highlights.title: Rice
highlights.description: The word for rice and the word for a meal are the same. Deepwater varieties grow with the flood; rainfed paddy fills the rest of the country.

highlights.label: Tonle Sap
highlights.title: Prahok
highlights.description: Fermented fish paste, made in the open each December from the migration out of the lake. It is under almost every savoury dish here.

highlights.label: Nationwide
highlights.title: Kroeung
highlights.description: Lemongrass, galangal, turmeric, kaffir lime and garlic pounded to a paste — the starting point for curries, soups and amok alike.

highlights.label: Nationwide
highlights.title: Fish Amok
highlights.description: Freshwater fish folded through kroeung and coconut, then steamed in banana leaf until it sets like a custard.

highlights.label: Nationwide
highlights.title: Num Banh Chok
highlights.description: Fermented rice noodles under a green fish gravy, sold from shoulder baskets and gone by eight in the morning.

highlights.label: Nationwide
highlights.title: Samlor Korko
highlights.description: A thick stew of whatever the garden has, bound with toasted ground rice — the dish most Cambodians name first.

highlights.label: Kampot · Kep
highlights.title: Kampot Pepper
highlights.description: One of the country's first two geographical indications, and the reason Kep crab tastes the way it does.

highlights.label: Kampong Speu
highlights.title: Palm Sugar
highlights.description: The other founding GI — sap tapped from sugar palms at dawn and boiled down by the roadside all morning.

name: Eco-Community Tourism
nameKh: ទេសចរណ៍ធម្មជាតិ និងសហគមន៍
tagline: Homestays, community forests and locally run enterprises.
summary: Homestays, community forests and locally run enterprises where the money from your trip stays in the village.
aboutTitle: Travel That Stays in the Village
coreIdentity: Community-based ecotourism, where the enterprise is owned by the village rather than sold to it — homestays taken in rotation, guiding and ranger work replacing logging income, and a share of every booking going into a fund the community spends itself.
highlightIntro: Nearly every site in this region runs on the same six-part model. It is worth understanding before you book, because it is what your money is actually buying.

highlights.label: Ownership
highlights.title: The community runs it
highlights.description: An elected committee sets prices, handles bookings and decides how income is divided — not an operator in Phnom Penh.

highlights.label: Rotation
highlights.title: Guests take turns
highlights.description: Homestays receive visitors on a roster, so the income spreads across the village instead of concentrating in three houses.

highlights.label: Employment
highlights.title: The people who knew the forest
highlights.description: Guiding, boat handling and patrol work goes to the households who previously logged, snared or fished it — the ones who know it best.

highlights.label: Revenue
highlights.title: A share of every booking
highlights.description: A fixed cut of each stay goes to a village fund, typically spent on the school, the water supply or the road.

highlights.label: Protection
highlights.title: The land agreement
highlights.description: Most sites sit on a Community Protected Area or community forest, held under agreement with the Ministry of Environment.

highlights.label: The trade-off
highlights.title: Logging, snaring, clearing
highlights.description: The model only holds while tourism pays better than the alternatives. Visiting in the low season is worth more than visiting in the high one.

name: Luxury Tourism
nameKh: ទេសចរណ៍ប្រណីត
tagline: Boutique retreats, private guides and time to do less.
summary: Boutique retreats, private guides and the slower, quieter version of every route above.
coreIdentity: The same country at a different pace. What the premium actually buys here is rarely marble — it is access before the coaches arrive, a guide who reads the inscriptions rather than reciting them, and the distance between an island jetty and anyone else.
highlightIntro: High-end infrastructure is concentrated in six places. This is what the top end looks like in each of them.

highlights.label: Siem Reap
highlights.title: The temple town
highlights.description: The deepest concentration of boutique and five-star properties in the country, plus the guides, courses and helicopters that come with them.

highlights.label: Preah Sihanouk
highlights.title: The Koh Rong archipelago
highlights.description: Whole-island properties reached by private launch, where the nearest other guests are a headland away.

highlights.label: Phnom Penh
highlights.title: The capital
highlights.description: Riverside hotels, the country's most ambitious kitchens, and the departure point for every Mekong cabin cruise.

highlights.label: Kampot · Kep
highlights.title: The southern retreats
highlights.description: Small properties with the Bokor range behind them and the crab market down the road — quiet rather than grand.

highlights.label: Koh Kong
highlights.title: The Cardamoms
highlights.description: Tented camps on the Tatai river whose rates fund the ranger patrols working the forest around them.

highlights.label: Kandal · Kratié
highlights.title: The Mekong
highlights.description: Cabin cruises running between the capital, the Tonle Sap and the delta below the Vietnamese border.
